title: The Black Cat
focus: self-destruction and the urge to do wrong

teacherSummary.text: On the night before his execution, the narrator recounts how drink turned him from a gentle animal-lover into a violent man. He blinds and then hangs his cat Pluto; his house burns, leaving the image of a cat on a wall. A second, similar cat appears, with a white patch that slowly takes the shape of a gallows. Trying to kill it, he murders his wife with an axe and walls her body up in the cellar. When police search, he raps on the wall, and the cat's howl reveals the corpse; he had walled the cat in with her.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The Black Cat,” how does Poe show self-destruction and the urge to do wrong? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The Black Cat, how does Poe develop the idea of self-destruction and the urge to do wrong? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the point of view in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Black Cat develops the idea of self-destruction and the urge to do wrong. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The Black Cat (where it begins, turns and ends) and its point of view shape the reader's understanding of self-destruction and the urge to do wrong. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Black Cat suggests about self-destruction and the urge to do wrong. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's point of view and symbolism), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Edgar Allan Poe uses point of view in The Black Cat to complicate the reader's understanding of self-destruction and the urge to do wrong. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Black Cat within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of self-destruction and the urge to do wrong responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Black Cat alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of self-destruction and the urge to do wrong follows or bends those conventions, using the point of view as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Black Cat and its treatment of self-destruction and the urge to do wrong. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's point of view and symbolism, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Black Cat as evidence for a larger claim about self-destruction and the urge to do wrong in The Black Cat. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Black Cat as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of self-destruction and the urge to do wrong. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Black Cat.

followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

items.text: Where does irony appear, and how does it connect this story to the larger concern with guilt and perversity?
items.lookFor: Look for gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The narrator blames outside forces, but the story shows his crimes come from his own choices. Useful evidence: “And then came, as if to my final and irrevocable overthrow, the spirit of Perverseness” (The Black Cat, paragraph 9): His theory of motive. On irony: His boastful rapping on the wall that hides the corpse summons the cat's cry. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

items.text: Background: Published in 1843 in the Saturday Evening Post, it appeared amid the temperance movement, which blamed alcohol for domestic violence. How does knowing this change the way you read one moment in the story?

items.text: A critic might argue: “Poe's idea of 'perverseness', the urge to do wrong because it is wrong, anticipates later psychology.” How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the story.

followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Sensitive content: Animal cruelty, murder of a wife, alcohol abuse. Preview the story, tell students in advance, and allow a pass on reading aloud. Keep discussion on how the writer uses these elements, not on graphic detail.
contentNotes.studentPreview: Heads-up: this story includes animal cruelty, murder of a wife, alcohol abuse.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “Why does the writer include this, and what does it make us notice?”
